opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question I think about a lot, and I don't think there's one right answer. I'd push back a little on the framing that these are opposed. Some of the most interesting scientific questions right now come out of the engineering of large models. When you scale something up and it starts doing things you didn't expect, that's a phenomenon that needs explaining, and explaining it is core deep learning research.

That said, I do worry about the field collapsing onto one recipe. Right now the default answer to almost any problem is "take a Transformer, make it bigger, train it on more data." That works remarkably well, and I don't want to be the person who says it won't keep working. But it means a lot of people are optimizing within a very narrow design space, and it's hard to know whether that space is actually the right one or just the one where we happened to invest all our engineering effort. The Transformer itself won partly because it fit the hardware so well, not purely because it was the best inductive bias.

So I think there's real value in people deliberately working on alternatives: different architectures, things like state space models, different ways of handling long context, approaches that are more efficient or more structured. Even if most of those don't beat the mainstream, they tell us something about which parts of the current recipe actually matter. And sometimes one of them does pan out, and then the whole field benefits.

The practical challenge, especially in academia, is that we can't compete on raw scale with industry labs, so we have to be smart about where we spend effort. To me that means picking questions where a small-scale experiment is actually informative, building good open tools and baselines so others can reproduce and extend things, and being honest about whether a result is likely to hold up at scale. I'd also encourage students not to treat "it doesn't beat GPT on a leaderboard" as the bar for whether an idea is worth pursuing. Understanding why something works, or failing in an interesting way, is a real contribution.

So my answer would be: let the people with the compute push scale, because we learn a lot from that, but the field needs a healthy portion of researchers asking the more fundamental questions, and those two groups should be talking to each other a lot more than they sometimes do.

r001.rationale: The response says unexpected behaviors and alternative architectures can yield useful research, but it does not state that significant shifts in deep learning’s core questions remain possible.

r002.rationale: It encourages researchers and students to pursue fundamental questions and ideas that do not beat GPT on a leaderboard, supporting work beyond simply scaling or improving efficiency.

r003.rationale: The response describes Transformers as the current default and says scaling works well, but makes no prediction that Transformers will remain dominant over the next three years.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So I think the honest answer is that it's not really a dichotomy I feel comfortable with, even though it's the framing everyone uses right now. Scaling isn't just engineering. The people doing it well are answering genuine scientific questions about what happens when you push compute and data, and those answers have surprised almost everyone, including me. I was pretty wrong about how far pure scaling of transformers would go, and I think it's worth saying that out loud.

That said, I do worry about what it does to the field's culture. If the only thing that counts as a result is a bigger number on a benchmark from a bigger model, then most academic labs are structurally shut out, and that's a problem not because academics deserve a seat but because you lose a certain kind of exploration. The transformer itself didn't come from someone scaling an LSTM. It came from people asking a pretty narrow question about attention and whether recurrence was actually necessary. Those questions tend to get asked by people who can't afford the big run and so have to think harder about why something works.

So the balance I'd argue for is something like: take scaling seriously as a scientific fact, don't be in denial about it, but keep a serious investment in understanding. Why does in-context learning emerge? What's actually happening in the attention patterns? Can we get the same behavior with linear-time models, or with structured state spaces, or with much smaller models trained differently? A lot of my own work recently has been in that direction, trying to find alternatives to attention that scale differently, and whether or not those end up winning, you learn a lot about the problem by trying.

The other thing I'd say is that the core deep learning questions and the engineering questions are converging in interesting ways. Things like how you parallelize a model, how you handle long context, how you do inference efficiently, those are now deeply tied to architectural choices. So a student who thinks about systems and a student who thinks about modeling are increasingly working on the same problem. I'd encourage people not to pick a camp. Learn to read the big-model results carefully, be skeptical about what they actually show, and then go find the small, sharp question that nobody with a huge cluster is going to bother asking.

r001.rationale: The response encourages exploring alternatives and says that trying them can teach researchers about the problem, but it does not clearly state that significant shifts in deep learning’s core questions remain possible.

r002.rationale: It advocates investing in understanding and pursuing “small, sharp” questions, including alternatives to attention, rather than treating larger benchmark scores as the only worthwhile results.

r003.rationale: The response does not predict whether Transformers will remain NLP’s dominant architecture over the next three years.

astra-6.text:
I think you want a field where both kinds of work can happen. Scaling up is scientifically interesting: you build something bigger, it starts doing things you didn’t expect, and that gives you new questions. The engineering can reveal things that you wouldn’t have discovered working only with small models.

But I worry when that becomes the only definition of progress. If every paper has to beat the strongest existing system, then trying a new architecture becomes very difficult. You’re comparing an early idea against something that has benefited from years of tuning and enormous resources. That’s a useful comparison for choosing a system to deploy, but it doesn’t necessarily tell you whether the idea is worth pursuing.

So I’d like to see more room for work that makes a clear claim and tests it carefully. Can we explain why a component works? Can we make training more efficient? Can we build in a useful assumption about language? Those are valuable contributions even if they don’t immediately produce the best benchmark score. And ideally there’s a feedback loop: the big systems expose problems, and the architectural work gives us new ways to address them.

r002.rationale: It calls for more room for carefully tested work on architectures, components, training, and language assumptions, even when that work does not immediately achieve the best benchmark score.

r003.rationale: It makes no prediction about Transformers or their dominance over the next three years.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we need both, and I worry a little when we treat them as competing goals. Building larger models has taught us a tremendous amount. There are questions you just can’t answer at a small scale, and getting those systems to work is itself a serious research challenge.

But I also think it’s important that we don’t make scale the only measure of progress. If every research idea requires training the biggest possible model, it becomes very difficult for a student or a small academic group to explore something different. And you can end up keeping the architecture fixed because changing it makes the engineering harder, even when the architecture is exactly what you want to investigate.

For me, the interesting work connects those two sides. Can you isolate a question about how a model learns or represents language, study it in a setting where you can run careful experiments, and then test whether the insight carries over? A small experiment doesn’t automatically tell you what will happen at scale, but it can give you a much better question to ask when you get there.

So I’d want a field with room for people building very large systems and people questioning the assumptions underneath them. We should be able to value a useful architectural idea or a clear explanation of a learning phenomenon, even if it doesn’t immediately produce the best benchmark number.

r002.rationale: It advocates making room for researchers to question assumptions and explore architectural ideas beyond simply scaling models or improving benchmark scores.
